paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 289
paragraphs.text: ALCAEUS 34(a)

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 289
paragraphs.text:
From P. Oxy. 1233 fr. 4 with additions from 2166(b) 3, 9. There
were probably three more stanzas, of which a mere half-dozen
letters remain. We possess two other hymns to the Dioscuri,
Homeric Hymn 33 (which need not be earlier than Alcaeus’
poem) and Theocritus 22. 1–26, and many of the elements of
Alcaeus’ poem are to be found in them. The poem is sometimes
thought to have been a prayer for a safe voyage, but it may have
been a prayer for Mytilene in distress, another example of the ship
of state metaphor.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 289
paragraphs.text:
Metre: Sapphic stanza, for which see note on Sappho 1. In
Alcaeus the fourth syllable of lines 1–3 is more often long than in
Sappho; diaeresis after the fifth syllable is commoner than in
Sappho. Note synizesis in 11 ἀργαλέ͜ᾳ.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 289
paragraphs.text: 1. δεῦτέ μοι: cf. Sapph. 128 δεῦτέ νυν ἄβραι Χάριτες.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 289
paragraphs.text:
νᾶσον Πέλοπος: so Tyrt. 2.4 Πέλοπος νῆσον, Cypr. fr. 11, but
cf. h. Ap. 250 Πελοπόννησον, Hes. fr. 189 M.-W. The
Dioscuri were associated with Sparta: cf. Theocr. 22.5
Λακεδαιμονίους δύ’ ἀδελφούς.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 289
paragraphs.text: 2. ἴφθιμοι: ἄλκιμοι is another possibility.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 289
paragraphs.text:
ἠδέ: like 7 �ῆα Epic, not Lesbian. Note too the number of
traditional epithets in the hymn: 5 εὔρηαν χθόνα, 6 ὠκυ-

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 290
paragraphs.text:
πόδων . . . ἵππων, 8 θανάτω . . . ζακρυόεντος (see note there),
9 εὐσδύγων . . . νάων, 12 νᾶϊ μελαίνᾳ.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 290
paragraphs.text: 3. εὐνόῳ: cf. 129.9–10 εὔνοον | θῦμον σκέθοντες.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 290
paragraphs.text:
8. ζακρυόεντος (=δια-): a well-placed epithet. Homer applies
the simple κρυόεις to φόβος and ἰωκή, Hesiod to πόλε-
μος.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 290
paragraphs.text:
9. ἐπ’: ὂν (=ἀνά) is possible, but less likely if πρότον’ ὀντρέ-
χοντες is correct in the next line.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 290
paragraphs.text:
10. πῆλοθεν λάμπροι: the reference here and in 11 φάος φέροντες
is to St. Elmo’s fire, the electrical discharge which creates a
glow about the mast-head and rigging of ships: the glow
was regarded as the epiphany of the Dioscuri. Xenophanes
said that the phenomenon was caused by little clouds
ignited by motion (Aetius II.18.1 =D.-K. A39).

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 290
paragraphs.text:
πρότον’ ὀντρέχοντες: Bowra’s brilliant supplement, ‘running
along the fore-stays’. πρότονοι is the Homeric form, but the
neuter is known from Et. Gud. 483.13.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 290
paragraphs.text:
11. φάος: in its literal sense, no doubt, but Homer used it several
times metaphorically for ‘deliverance’, e.g. Il. 17.615 καὶ
τῷ μὲν φάος ἦλθεν.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 34a, p. 290
paragraphs.text:
12. μελαίνᾳ: the conventional epithet may have some point
here: the blackness of the ship is in contrast to the brilliance
and light of the Dioscuri.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 293
paragraphs.text: ALCAEUS 129

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 293
paragraphs.text:
P. Oxy. 2165 fr. 1 col. i 1–32; a little information is added by
2166(c) 6. The fragment, one of our two longest pieces of Alcaeus,
is an example of his ‘stasiotic’ verse: in exile somewhere on Lesbos,
he cries to Zeus, Hera (?) and Dionysus for vengeance on Pittacus
the traitor.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 293
paragraphs.text: Metre: Alcaic stanza.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text:
1. τόδε: Alcaeus represents himself as speaking in the pre-
cinct: cf. 6 σέ, 8 τόνδε (if that is the correct reading).

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text:
2. εὔδειλον: only here for εὐδείελος, Homer’s epithet for
Ithaca (e.g. Od. 2.167 Ἰθάκην εὐδείελον), variously
explained as ‘clear, distinct’ (cf. δῆλος), or ‘fair, i.e. sunny,
in the afternoon’ (δείλη).

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text:
τέμενος: the sanctuary may have been at Cape Phokas on the
S. coast of the island: Jerome D. Quinn, A.J.A. 65 (1961),
391–3, pl. 128–9; other sites are suggested by Louis Robert,
R.E.A. 62 (1960), 285 ff and J. M. Cook, C.A.H. II (rev.
ed. 1961), ch. 38, 7.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text:
3. ξῦνον: ‘common’ either to the three divinities or to all
Lesbians.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: κάτεσσαν = καθεῖσαν, aor. of καθίζω.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text:
4. ἔθηκαν: a marginal note should probably be read as ζεθηκα,
which suggests a variant reading ζέθηκα(ν) = διέθηκαν.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text:
5. κἀπωνύμασσαν = καὶ ἐπωνόμασαν; ‘they entitled Zeus “An-
tiaeus”.’

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: ἀντίαον: ἀντίᾱος is Lesbian for ἀνταῖος, which presumably

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: means the same as ἀνταῖος, ‘invoked by suppliants.’ A marginal note here seems to explain the adj. as ἱκέσιον. Cf. Sapph. 17.9 Δί’ ἀντ[ in a passage which refers to the same trinity, Hera, Zeus, Dionysus, as Alcaeus here.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: 6. Αἰολήαν: i.e. goddess of Aeolus, who gave his name to the Aeolians.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: θέον: the goddess is presumably Hera. We might not have guessed it from the present description alone, although Orph. Hymn 16.4 has παντογένεθλος of Hera; but Sappho 17 says that the Atridae, returning home from Troy, invoked Hera, Zeus and Dionysus on Lesbos.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: 7. πάντων γενέθλαν: for γενέθλα, ‘mother’ instead of the usual ‘child, family’, cf. Il. 2.857 ἀργύρου . . . γενέθλη of a silvermine.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: τέρτον: Aeolic for τρίτον.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: 8. τόνδε κεμήλιον: cf. 1n. κεμήλιον, however, is unexplained, and Beattie’s τὸν Σεμελήϊον is attractive.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: 9. Ζόννυσσον=Διόνυσον.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 294
paragraphs.text: ὠμήσταν: ‘eater of raw flesh’. ὠμοφαγία was the climax of the

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
midwinter Dionysiac rite: see Dodds, Bacchae, 2nd ed.,
xvi–xx.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
10. ἄρας: the term may include both the prayer of 11–12 and the
imprecation of 13–14.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
13. Ὕρραον = Ὑρραῖον and Ὕρραον . . . παῖδα = ‘son of Hyrrhas’,
i.e. Pittacus. The adj. is elsewhere always Ὑρράδιος.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
14. κήνων Ἐρίννυς: ‘their avenger’: κήνων: presumably those
who have lost their lives because of Pittacus’ treachery. In
Il. 19.259–60 the Erinyes are avengers of perjury: cf. Hes.
Op. 803–4. For the genitive κήνων cf. Od. 11.280 μητρὸς
Ἐρίνυες.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text: ὤς ποτ’ κτλ.: ‘since once we swore’.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
17. γᾶν ἐπέμμενοι (=Homeric ἐπιειμένοι): ‘clad in earth’:
the same metaphor at Pi. N. 11.16 γᾶν ἐπιεσσόμενος and
elsewhere.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text: 18. ἐπικ . . ην: no known verb fits the traces.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
19. ἤπειτα=ἢ ἔπειτα, ‘or else’, which in Homer normally
introduces the less desirable alternative; cf. Od. 20.63
however.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
21. φύσγων=φύσκων, ‘pot-belly.’ Diogenes Laertius 1.81 gives a
list of epithets applied by Alcaeus to Pittacus: σαράπους
and σάραπος (splay-footed), χειροπόδης (with chapped
feet), γαύρηξ (boaster), φύσκων and γάστρων (big-belly),
ζοφοδορπίδας (sup-by-night?), ἀγάσυρτος (dirty).

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
22. οὐ διελέξατο κτλ.: perhaps ‘he did not discuss these things
with his heart’, i.e. ‘he did not take them to heart’; the gen-
κήνων must be explained by analogy with ἐνθυμεῖσθαι.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text:
πόσιν κτλ.: oaths are similarly trampled underfoot at Il.
4.157 κατὰ δ’ ὅρκια πιστὰ πάτησαν, Archil. 79a.13 λὰξ δ’ ἐφ’
ὁρκίοις ἔβη.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 295
paragraphs.text: 23. δάπτει: ‘devours’, like a ravening animal: Homer has the

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
verb of a lion (Il. 11.481) and wolves (Il. 16.159); cf. Il.
23.183. Alc. 70.7 has δαπτέτω πόλιν of Pittacus.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 129, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
24. Little can be gleaned from the scraps of 24–8. κὰν νόμον (25)
=κατὰ νόμον. γλαύκας (26) might be followed by Ἀ[θανάας
(Diehl), or might qualify Ἥρας. Myrsilus seems to have
been mentioned in 28. The coronis in the margin marks 32
as the last line of the poem.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text: ALCAEUS 130

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
From the same source as the last piece, P. Oxy. 2165, fr. 1, col.
ii 9–28. Another poem written in exile, incomplete and difficult
but full of interest.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
Metre: an aeolic stanza. If lines 3 and 4 are considered as one,
they give a glyconic + lesser asclepiad.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
16. Since the metre of the previous lines, little of which survives,
was almost certainly different, it is probable that a new
poem begins at this point, although there is no coronis in
the margin. But what the first words could have been is
anyone’s guess.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text: 17. ἀγροϊωτίκαν: only here: Sapph. 57.1, 2 has ἀγροΐωτις.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
19. καρυζομένας = κηρυσσομένης, ‘longing to hear the Assembly
being summoned’.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text: Ὦγεσιλαΐδα = ὦ Ἀγεσιλαΐδα; we do not know who Agesilaidas

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text: was.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text: 20. βόλλας=βουλῆς.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
21. The text is difficult. Lobel suggests that the pap. had κακγε-
γήρασ’=καταγεγήρασι, ‘they have grown old’, but γέγηρα is
unknown, and -ᾱσι for Lesbian -αισι is unparalleled.
Page’s suggestion that the writer intended κἀπὶ γῆρας and
that the verb, probably ἔζων, came at the beginning of 23 is
more attractive, but it seems to be incompatible with the
traces and ἔζων gives an anomalous contracted form for
ἔζωον: no other verb fits the beginning of 23.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
τωνδέων: Aeolic gen. plur. of ὅδε with double flexion: cf.
Homer’s τοίσδεσι, τοίσδεσσι.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text: 22. ἀλλαλοκάκων: ‘hurting each other’.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 296
paragraphs.text:
24. ἐσχατίαισ’: ‘in the outlying districts, at the back of beyond’;
cf. 328 καί τις ἐπ’ ἐσχατίαισιν οἰκεῖς.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 297
paragraphs.text:
Ὀνυμακλέης: Onomacles is unknown: presumably he was a
recluse or exile.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 297
paragraphs.text:
25. λυκαιμίαις: only here, unless Hsch. λυκαιχλίας is a corrup-
tion of it. Page suggests a derivation from λύκος and αἰμός,
‘thicket’ (Hsch. αἰμοί· δρυμοί): λυκαιμίαις may be nom.
sing. masc., ‘I, a wolf-thicket man’, or acc. plur., object of
ἐοίκησα, ‘I settled in the wolf-thickets.’

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 297
paragraphs.text:
27. ὀννέλην = ἀνελεῖν: ‘to get rid of, give up (?)’ strife. But what
precedes is quite uncertain, and ἄμεινον is unmetri-
cal.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 297
paragraphs.text:
28. τέμενος θέων: probably the sanctuary of Zeus, Hera and
Dionysus mentioned in 129.2 ff.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 297
paragraphs.text:
30. αὔταις: dat. pl., not acc. pl.: cf. 308(b).2 κορύφαισιν ἄγναις,
Sapph. 160.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 297
paragraphs.text:
32. κριννόμεναι φύαν: Theophrastus ap. Ath. 13.610a mentions
women’s beauty competitions on Tenedos and Lesbos,
Schol. A Hom. Il. 9.129 says that the competition on
Lesbos, the καλλιστεῖα, was held ἐν τῷ τῆς Ἥρας τεμένει.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 130, p. 297
paragraphs.text: 34. ἄχω θεσπεσία: so at Sapph. 44.27.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 298
paragraphs.text: ALCAEUS 326

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 298
paragraphs.text:
Quoted like fr. 6.1–3 by Heraclitus, All. 5, as an example of
allegory: the first impression, that the lines describe an actual
storm at sea, is not to be trusted, he says: the poem is about
Myrsilus and his ‘tyrannical’ conspiracy against the Mytileneans.
Page (S. & A. 185–7) completes l. 9 with τὰ δ’ ὀή̣[ϊα from a com-
mentary on Alcaeus, P. Oxy. 2306 (=L.-P. 305), col. ii.20, and
adds to it another papyrus fragment, P. Oxy. 2297, fr. 5 (=L.-P.
208(a)).

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 298
paragraphs.text: Metre: Alcaic stanza.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 298
paragraphs.text:
1. ἀσυννέτημμι: an uncommon word; Hippocrates has ἀσυνετέω
(Fract. 25).

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 298
paragraphs.text:
στάσιν: the word suggests both the direction from which the
winds blow (cf. Hdt. 2.26) and their strife, and may also
point forward to the allegory.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 298
paragraphs.text:
2. κῦμα κυλίνδεται: so at Il. 11.307. In 4 νᾶϊ . . . μελαίνᾳ is
also Homeric: cf. 34(a).12.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 298
paragraphs.text: 6. πὲρ . . . ἔχει = ὑπερέχει, ‘covers’; cf. Sapph. 16.6, 96.9.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 298
paragraphs.text: 7. ζάδηλον = διάδηλον, another uncommon word, here ‘trans-

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 299
paragraphs.text:
parent’ (thanks to the great gaps in the sail); cf. Hor. Od.
1.14.9 non tibi sunt integra lintea.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 299
paragraphs.text: 9. χόλαισι =χαλῶσι, ἄγκονναι =ἄγκοιναι, ropes of some kind.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 326, p. 299
paragraphs.text: ὀήϊα =Homer’s οἰήϊα, ‘rudders’.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 302
paragraphs.text: ALCAEUS 350

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 302
paragraphs.text: 1–2 are from Hephaestion Ench. x 3 and Libanius Or. 13.5, the rest composed by Ahrens, Hoffmann and O. Müller from Strabo’s paraphrase (13.617) : τὸν ἀδελφὸν Ἀντιμενίδαν, ὅν φησιν Ἀλκαῖος Βαβυλωνίοις συμμαχοῦντα τελέσαι μέγαν ἆθλον καὶ ἐκ πόνων αὐτοὺς ῥύσασθαι κτείναντα ἄνδρα μαχαίταν βασιληΐων παλαιστάν, ὥς φησιν, ἀπολείποντα μόνον μίαν παχέων ἀπὺ πέμπων. A poem of welcome to Alcaeus’ brother, Antimenidas, who seems to have served as a mercenary in the Babylonian army; this may have been during the series of Nebuchadrezzar’s campaigns in Palestine at the beginning of the 6th century (II Kings 24–5), since another fragment of Alcaeus (48.10–11) mentions ‘holy Babylon’ and Ascalon together.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 302
paragraphs.text: Metre: lesser Asclepiad.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 302
paragraphs.text: 1. ἐκ περάτων γᾶς: so in Th. 1.69.5; cf. Il. 8.478–9 πείρατα . . . γαίης.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 302
paragraphs.text: ἐλαφαντίναν κτλ.: ‘with the ivory hilt of your sword bound with gold’.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 302
paragraphs.text: 5. βασιληΐων κτλ.: ‘lacking only one palm’s breadth of five

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 303
paragraphs.text:
royal cubits’: the warrior stood about 8 ft. 4 in.; for the
royal cubit see Hdt. 1.178.3. Hdt.’s description of Ar-
tachaees, the tallest soldier in the Persian army, is close to
Alcaeus: ἀπὸ γὰρ πέντε πήχεων βασιληίων ἀπέλειπε τέσσαρας
δακτύλους.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 303
paragraphs.text: ἴαν = μίαν.

paragraphs.citation: Campbell, Greek Lyric Poetry (1967), Alcaeus 350, p. 303
paragraphs.text: πέμπων: note the declension of the numeral πέμπε.
